intro: Here's what happens from having your site on your computer to it being an address you can send over WhatsApp: who sees it, what it costs, what each company is, and how to undo things when something goes wrong.

preguntas.q: The website the chat built for me, is it already online?
preguntas.a: No. Nobody but you can see it yet. What you have is a file saved on your computer, or a preview inside the conversation itself. It opens with a double-click and it works, but it only works there. For it to exist on the internet, that file has to be placed on another company's computer that's on twenty-four hours a day. That's called hosting, and it's a separate step you have to take yourself. Until you do, your website is like a dish cooked in your own kitchen: it exists, it smells great, but nobody off the street can walk in and try it.
preguntas.corta: No. It's on your computer. Publishing it is a separate step.

preguntas.q: I sent my sister the address starting with localhost and she got an error. What did I do wrong?
preguntas.a: Nothing. That address doesn't work outside your computer and never will. Localhost literally means "this computer." When your sister types localhost:3000 into her phone, her phone looks for itself, not for you, and that's why she gets an error. That's correct behavior. On top of that, that address only lives while the program serving your site is running: shut down your computer and it disappears. To send something to someone you need a public address, which is a different thing you get by publishing.
preguntas.corta: Nothing. Localhost is just your computer, it doesn't travel.

preguntas.q: How do I get a real address I can send over WhatsApp?
preguntas.a: By dragging a folder, without typing anything. Put your file in a folder, and that file has to be named index.html. Go to app.netlify.com/drop and drop the folder there. In about twenty seconds you get an address like happy-cakes-1a2b3c.netlify.app that opens on any phone in the world. That odd name in the middle is generated automatically. If you want to keep it and update it later, it'll ask you to create a free account; for a one-off test, not even that.
preguntas.corta: Drag the folder to app.netlify.com/drop and you have an address.

preguntas.q: Netlify, Vercel, GitHub... I'm lost. Which is which?
preguntas.a: GitHub stores, Netlify and Vercel display. GitHub is the archive: your project lives there with its whole history, snapshot by snapshot, and that's where you get the rollback from. It's not a website people can use, it's the stored code. Netlify and Vercel do the other job: they take your project and turn it into a public website with its own address. Between those two, for what you're going to do, the difference doesn't matter much. Netlify has the drag-and-drop route, the easiest of all. Vercel connects to GitHub and republishes automatically every time you push something.
preguntas.corta: GitHub stores your project. Netlify and Vercel publish it.

preguntas.q: Is this going to cost me money?
preguntas.a: For what you'll do in the course, no. GitHub has a free plan and doesn't ask for a card. Netlify and Vercel have free plans that easily handle a personal site or a small business's; on Vercel it's called Hobby and you have to pick it manually, since the dashboard nudges you toward the paid one. The one thing that does cost money from day one is a nice-sounding domain name, and only if you want one. Once the project truly grows and gets a lot of traffic, that's when you start paying: Vercel's paid plan runs around $20 a month, but check their site, since prices move.
preguntas.corta: Not to get started. The free tier is plenty at first.

preguntas.q: And is it free forever?
preguntas.a: Nobody can promise you that. Free plans exist because it's in these companies' interest to get you started there, and they change the terms whenever they want. What's true today: as long as it's just you and a few people you know visiting your site, you won't pay anything. The classic trap with these services isn't that they cut you off, it's that if you've entered a card, they start billing you for overage, and overage is measured in visits, which is exactly what you don't control. Before entering a card anywhere, check their settings for a "pause the project" option instead of getting charged.
preguntas.corta: Nobody can promise that. Today, yes; terms change.

preguntas.q: The address I got is ugly. How much does one like sweetcakes.com cost?
preguntas.a: It's the one guaranteed expense, and it's small: around $10-15 a year. That name is called a domain, and you don't buy it, you rent it by the year, so it has to be renewed. The exact price depends on the ending you pick (.com, .es) and where you buy it, so check on the seller's site before paying, don't trust a number from memory. Watch out for one very common trick: some sites give you a rock-bottom price the first year and bump it up considerably the second. Always look at the renewal price, not the introductory offer.
preguntas.corta: Around $10-15 a year, renewable.

preguntas.q: Do I have to buy the domain before publishing?
preguntas.a: No, and it's better if you don't. Publish first with the free address they give you, show it to three people, and check that the site really convinces you. The domain connects afterward, in ten minutes, and none of the project needs redoing: it's the same site, only the name you reach it by changes. Plenty of people spend the money on day one, pick the name in a rush, and regret it later. And once paid for, the domain is locked in for the whole year.
preguntas.corta: No. Publish free first; add the domain later.

preguntas.q: My phone number is on the site. Can anyone see it?
preguntas.a: Yes, anyone. Publishing means making it public, no caveats. Anyone with the link opens it, and on top of that, automated programs pass by too, gathering whatever they find, including ones that harvest phone numbers and emails to sell lists. Before publishing, read through your own site asking yourself what on it you wouldn't mind seeing pinned to the front door: your personal phone number, your home address, a client's name, your van's license plate. If you want people to reach you, a WhatsApp or email link works just as well and doesn't require displaying the number written out on the page.
preguntas.corta: Yes. Public is public, and bots read it too.

preguntas.q: I already took it off the site. So it's not online anymore, right?
preguntas.a: Not so fast. Taking it off your site is the first step, but not the last. Google and other search engines keep a copy of what they saw and can keep showing it for weeks. And if someone took a screenshot, or if your project is uploaded to GitHub, the data still exists in the history even if it doesn't show on the page today. That's why you plan for this beforehand, not after: removing something from the internet isn't a button you press, it's a wait. If what leaked was a key or a password, deleting it doesn't help anymore: it has to be revoked and replaced.
preguntas.corta: Not entirely. Google takes weeks to forget it.

preguntas.q: The AI broke half my site trying to fix a button. How do I go back to yesterday's version?
preguntas.a: If you'd uploaded it to GitHub, in two minutes. GitHub saves a full snapshot of your project every time you push something, with its date and note. Go to your repository, click where it says "Commits," find yesterday's snapshot, and tell the AI to bring the project back to that point. You haven't lost anything along the way. The other case is the problem: if you never uploaded it, there's no snapshot of yesterday anywhere and nothing to recover. That's why you push before asking for a big change, not after.
preguntas.corta: With GitHub, you're back to yesterday's snapshot in two minutes.

preguntas.q: I published something broken and a client is looking at it right now. Is there a panic button?
preguntas.a: Yes, and it takes under a minute. In Vercel, go to "Deployments," the list of every version you've published, each with its timestamp. Find an earlier one that worked, click the three dots on the right, and choose "Promote to Production" (on some accounts it shows as "Instant Rollback"). Your public address instantly starts showing that older version again. This doesn't touch your code at all: it stays exactly as it was, you're only changing which version is being shown. Afterward, calmly, fix the actual bug.
preguntas.corta: Yes. In Vercel, "Promote to Production" on a working version.

preguntas.q: Do I absolutely have to upload it to GitHub to publish?
preguntas.a: To publish, no. To sleep soundly, yes. If you drag the folder to Netlify, you publish without going through GitHub and it works perfectly fine. What you lose is the rollback: without GitHub there's no history, and the day the AI breaks something, yesterday's version to go back to doesn't exist. On top of that, connecting GitHub to Netlify or Vercel saves you the drag-and-drop: you push a change and the site updates itself in a couple of minutes, with no one to notify. It's worth doing early, not six months from now.
preguntas.corta: Not to publish; yes if you want to be able to roll back.

preguntas.q: It's asking whether the repository is public or private and I don't know what to pick.
preguntas.a: Private, always, at the start. Public means anyone in the world can read your whole project, file by file. And not just today's version: every old snapshot too. If a password or a payment key ever slipped into a file, it stays saved there even after you delete it later, and there are automated programs scanning GitHub specifically to find those. Making it public later is one click. Going back, once someone's copied it, isn't possible. Start closed.
preguntas.corta: Private. You can go public later; you can't undo it after someone's copied it.

preguntas.q: I think I uploaded a file with a key inside. Do I just delete it?
preguntas.a: No. Deleting it doesn't help: it has to be revoked. Removing the line from the file today doesn't remove it from the snapshot saved yesterday, and that snapshot stays in the history. And if the repository was public even for a moment, assume some automated bot already has a copy of it. The only thing that truly fixes this is called rotating: go to the website of the company that issued you that key, revoke it, and generate a new one. The old one stops working right then, no matter who has it. Do it now, not tomorrow.
preguntas.corta: No. You need to revoke that key and generate a new one.

preguntas.q: I see a red banner saying "Build Failed." Did I break the site?
preguntas.a: No. The version already published is still up and people are still seeing it. That banner just means one attempt to publish didn't go through, nothing more. And the first one almost always fails, for two boring reasons: your computer is more forgiving than the server, and the keys the project needs are stored in a file of yours that deliberately isn't uploaded, so the server doesn't have them there. The fix isn't understanding it: open "Build Logs," copy the last twenty or thirty lines, and paste them straight to the AI. That text is written for machines, not for you.
preguntas.corta: No. The published site is still alive. Paste it the error.

preguntas.q: I changed the title and the public address still shows the old one. Why?
preguntas.a: Almost always because the change hasn't arrived there yet. Your project lives in three places at once: your computer, GitHub's storage, and the public site. A change made on your computer stays only on your computer until you push it, and publishing takes a couple more minutes. So the first question is always the same: which of the three addresses am I actually looking at? If you've already pushed it and the dashboard says "Ready," then it's your browser showing you the cached copy: hard-refresh with Ctrl and F5 together (on Mac, Command, Shift, and R).
preguntas.corta: Either you haven't pushed it, or it's your browser.

preguntas.q: I open my own site from my phone and it asks me to log into Vercel. Is it published wrong?
preguntas.a: No, it's protected. Vercel can put a login screen in front of your site so only you get in, and on some accounts that comes turned on by default. It lets you through because you're logged in on your computer; a client sees that screen and leaves. Turn it off in the project dashboard: go to "Settings," then "Deployment Protection," and disable "Vercel Authentication." Test it afterward from your phone with wifi off, which is the only test that actually proves anything: if it opens like that, it opens for anyone.
preguntas.corta: It's protected. Turn off "Vercel Authentication" in Settings.

preguntas.q: My site has a contact form. Will the messages reach me?
preguntas.a: No. A standalone file doesn't send emails, no matter how much it looks like it does. The form displays, you can type into it, and the button clicks, but that goes nowhere: it needs a service behind it that collects what people write and delivers it to you, and that's contracted separately. It's the most expensive kind of failure, because your clients believe they've written to you and you never find out. Until you have that set up, remove the form and put in a WhatsApp link and an email link instead: they work from minute one and cost nothing.
preguntas.corta: No. Without a service behind it, that button sends nothing.

preguntas.q: Can I show localhost to a client in a meeting?
preguntas.a: Bad idea. Localhost only exists while your computer is on and the program is running, so it depends on nothing closing, on your wifi, and on your battery. And if you send the address for them to check later, it won't open for them at all. Publish first, even with the ugly free address, and send that link. It takes twenty seconds and saves you the scene of restarting things in front of a client. Localhost is where you get to be wrong for free; a meeting isn't.
preguntas.corta: Better not. Publish first and show them the public link.
